claim: Kv1.2 potassium channels are regulated by the amino acid transporter Slc7a5.
source: We recently reported powerful regulation of Kv1.2 potassium channels by the amino acid transporter Slc7a5.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract and introduction, referencing prior work by the authors.

claim: Kv1.1 channels are regulated by Slc7a5.
source: In this study, we report that Kv1.1 channels are also regulated by Slc7a5, albeit with different functional outcomes.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: Kv1.1 exhibits prominent current enhancement ('disinhibition') with holding potentials more negative than −120 mV in heterologous expression systems.
source: In heterologous expression systems, Kv1.1 exhibits prominent current enhancement ('disinhibition') with holding potentials more negative than −120 mV.
evidence: This is directly stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: Knockdown of endogenous Slc7a5 leads to larger Kv1.1 currents.
source: Knockdown of endogenous Slc7a5 leads to larger Kv1.1 currents and strongly attenuates the disinhibition effect, suggesting that Slc7a5 regulation of Kv1.1 involves channel inhibition that can be reversed by supraphysiological hyperpolarizing voltages.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in Figure 3.

claim: Knockdown of endogenous Slc7a5 strongly attenuates the disinhibition effect in Kv1.1.
source: Knockdown of endogenous Slc7a5 leads to larger Kv1.1 currents and strongly attenuates the disinhibition effect, suggesting that Slc7a5 regulation of Kv1.1 involves channel inhibition that can be reversed by supraphysiological hyperpolarizing voltages.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in Figure 3.

claim: Slc7a5 regulation of Kv1.1 involves channel inhibition that can be reversed by supraphysiological hyperpolarizing voltages.
source: Knockdown of endogenous Slc7a5 leads to larger Kv1.1 currents and strongly attenuates the disinhibition effect, suggesting that Slc7a5 regulation of Kv1.1 involves channel inhibition that can be reversed by supraphysiological hyperpolarizing voltages.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings stated in the abstract.

claim: Exchange of the voltage-sensing domain between Kv1.1 and Kv1.2 controls the sensitivity and response to Slc7a5.
source: We investigated chimeric combinations of Kv1.1 and Kv1.2, demonstrating that exchange of the voltage-sensing domain controls the sensitivity and response to Slc7a5, and localize a specific position in S1 with prominent effects on Slc7a5 sensitivity.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in Figures 7 and 8.

claim: A specific position in S1 has prominent effects on Slc7a5 sensitivity.
source: We investigated chimeric combinations of Kv1.1 and Kv1.2, demonstrating that exchange of the voltage-sensing domain controls the sensitivity and response to Slc7a5, and localize a specific position in S1 with prominent effects on Slc7a5 sensitivity.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in Figures 8 and 9.

claim: The voltage-sensing domain is a determinant of Slc7a5 modulation of Kv1 channels.
source: Overall, our study highlights multiple Slc7a5-sensitive Kv1 subunits, and identifies the voltage-sensing domain as a determinant of Slc7a5 modulation of Kv1 channels.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: Kv1.2 co-expression with Slc7a5 leads to a prominent shift (~−50 mV) of the voltage-dependence of activation.
source: Features of Slc7a5-dependent modulation of Kv1.2 currents include a pronounced shift (~−50 mV) of the voltage-dependence of activation, along with prominent inhibition of currents that is relieved by strong negative holding voltages.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by data in Figure 1A (dashed lines, data reproduced from Baronas et al., 2018).

claim: Slc7a5 causes prominent inhibition of Kv1.2 currents that is relieved by strong negative holding voltages.
source: Features of Slc7a5-dependent modulation of Kv1.2 currents include a pronounced shift (~−50 mV) of the voltage-dependence of activation, along with prominent inhibition of currents that is relieved by strong negative holding voltages.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by experimental data in Figure 2.

claim: Voltage-dependent relief of inhibition by Slc7a5 can exceed 10-fold enhancement of whole cell current.
source: This voltage-dependent relief of inhibition can be very pronounced, often exceeding 10-fold enhancement of whole cell current.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by experimental data in Figure 2.

claim: Certain epilepsy-linked mutations of Kv1.2 are hypersensitive to Slc7a5-mediated modulation.
source: Strikingly, certain epilepsy-linked mutations of Kv1.2 are hypersensitive to Slc7a5-mediated modulation, leading to extraordinarily large (sometimes >100 mV) gating shifts when co-expressed with Slc7a5 (Baronas et al., 2018; Masnada et al., 2017; EuroEPINOMICS RES consortium et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Epilepsy-linked mutations of Kv1.2 can lead to extraordinarily large (sometimes >100 mV) gating shifts when co-expressed with Slc7a5.
source: Strikingly, certain epilepsy-linked mutations of Kv1.2 are hypersensitive to Slc7a5-mediated modulation, leading to extraordinarily large (sometimes >100 mV) gating shifts when co-expressed with Slc7a5 (Baronas et al., 2018; Masnada et al., 2017; EuroEPINOMICS RES consortium et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Kv1.1 does not exhibit a significant shift in the voltage-dependence of activation in the presence of Slc7a5.
source: Our initial characterization of Kv1.1 did not reveal a significant shift in the voltage-dependence of activation in the presence of Slc7a5 (Figure 1A,B).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 1A,B.

claim: No statistical difference in voltage-dependent gating parameters were detected for Kv1.1±Slc7a5.
source: Fit parameters for Kv1.1 were (co-expression with Slc7a5 in parentheses): V1/2 = -34.9 ± 0.3 mV (−37.5 ± 0.2 mV); k = 6.9 ± 0.9 mV (7.3 ± 0.9 mV). No statistical difference in voltage-dependent gating parameters were detected for Kv1.1±Slc7a5.
evidence: This is stated in the Figure 1 legend and represents statistical analysis of the data.

claim: Kv1.2 expressed alone exhibits relatively large currents and no apparent relief of inhibition.
source: Kv1.2 expressed alone exhibits relatively large currents, and no apparent relief of inhibition (Figure 2A,C).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 2A,C.

claim: Kv1.2 co-expression with Slc7a5 leads to baseline currents that are small shortly after whole cell break-in but increase substantially after 20–30 s at a holding potential of −120 mV.
source: However, Kv1.2 co-expression with Slc7a5 (Figure 2A,D) leads to baseline currents that are small shortly after whole cell break-in but increase substantially after 20–30 s at a holding potential of −120 mV.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 2A,D.

claim: Kv1.2 with Slc7a5 exhibits an average 5.1 ± 2.2 fold current enhancement.
source: We observed an average 5.1 ± 2.2 fold (mean ± S.D.) current enhancement of Kv1.2 with Slc7a5, although this is variable and reached 11.5-fold in some cells (Figure 2C,D).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 2C,D.

claim: Kv1.1 exhibits prominent current enhancement even in the absence of co-transfected Slc7a5.
source: In contrast, this effect was prominent for Kv1.1 (Figure 2B), even in the absence of co-transfected Slc7a5 (Figure 2B), with an average current enhancement of 3.2 ± 1.2 fold (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 2B,E.

claim: Kv1.1 exhibits an average current enhancement of 3.2 ± 1.2 fold in the absence of co-transfected Slc7a5.
source: In contrast, this effect was prominent for Kv1.1 (Figure 2B), even in the absence of co-transfected Slc7a5 (Figure 2B), with an average current enhancement of 3.2 ± 1.2 fold (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 2B,E.

claim: Kv1.1 co-expressed with Slc7a5 exhibits a 6.1 ± 2.6 fold change in current enhancement.
source: These features (inhibition of baseline current, and relief of inhibition with −120 mV holding potential) became more prominent when Slc7a5 was co-expressed with Kv1.1, with a 6.1 ± 2.6 fold change (Figure 2B,F).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 2B,F.

claim: Slc7a5 causes prominent inhibition of both Kv1.1 and Kv1.2.
source: Taken together, these findings indicate that Slc7a5 causes prominent inhibition of both Kv1.1 and Kv1.2.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the results section based on the experimental data in Figure 2.

claim: Reversal of Slc7a5-mediated inhibition by strong hyperpolarizing voltages leads to enhancement of current.
source: Reversal of Slc7a5-mediated inhibition by strong hyperpolarizing voltages leads to enhancement of current.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the results section based on the experimental data in Figure 2.

claim: Kv1.1 is particularly sensitive to Slc7a5, leading to modulation by endogenous levels of Slc7a5 in a heterologous cell line.
source: At present, we have not determined whether there is reciprocal modulation of Slc7a5 function by Kv channels. However, this possibility will continue to be explored, as certain combinations of Kv7 channels and myo-inositol transporters exhibit mutual regulation, along with other channel:transporter combinations (Abbott et al., 2014; Lebowitz et al., 2019; Manville et al., 2017; Neverisky and Abbott, 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by experimental data in Figure 3.

claim: The ShR4-1 cell line exhibits prominent knockdown of Slc7a5 as confirmed by qPCR and Western blot.
source: We selected a cell line (ShR4-1) with prominent knockdown of Slc7a5, confirmed by qPCR and Western blot (Figure 3A–C).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 3A-C.

claim: Expression of Kv1.1 in ShR4-1 cells generated larger currents relative to parental LM cells.
source: Expression of Kv1.1 in ShR4-1 cells generated larger currents relative to parental LM cells, and although some modest Kv1.1 current disinhibition persisted in ShR4-1 cells (Figure 3F), the magnitude of this effect was significantly attenuated relative to parental LM cells (Figure 3G).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 3F,G.

claim: The magnitude of Kv1.1 current disinhibition was significantly attenuated in ShR4-1 cells relative to parental LM cells.
source: Expression of Kv1.1 in ShR4-1 cells generated larger currents relative to parental LM cells, and although some modest Kv1.1 current disinhibition persisted in ShR4-1 cells (Figure 3F), the magnitude of this effect was significantly attenuated relative to parental LM cells (Figure 3G).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 3F,G.

claim: Knockdown of Slc7a5 in the ShR4-1 cell line did not affect Kv1.1 voltage-dependent activation relative to parental LM cells.
source: Knockdown of Slc7a5 in the ShR4-1 cell line did not affect Kv1.1 voltage-dependent activation relative to parental LM cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 2), confirming that Kv1.1 and Kv1.2 exhibit distinct functional responses to Slc7a5.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Kv1.1 and Kv1.2 exhibit distinct functional responses to Slc7a5.
source: Knockdown of Slc7a5 in the ShR4-1 cell line did not affect Kv1.1 voltage-dependent activation relative to parental LM cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 2), confirming that Kv1.1 and Kv1.2 exhibit distinct functional responses to Slc7a5.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the results section based on the experimental data.

claim: Human Slc7a5 transcript is resistant to the mouse-targeted shRNA sequence used for the ShR4-1 cell line, due to two base pair mismatches.
source: The human Slc7a5 transcript is resistant to the mouse-targeted shRNA sequence used for the ShR4-1 cell line, due to two base pair mismatches.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and explains the experimental design for rescue experiments.

claim: Transfection with human Slc7a5 cDNA rescued Kv1.1 modulation in ShR4-1 cells similar to parental LM cells.
source: Thus, we could rescue Slc7a5 expression in ShR4-1 cells by transfection with human Slc7a5 cDNA (~91% sequence identity, Figure 3B,E–G). This rescued Kv1.1 modulation similar to parental LM cells (Figure 3E), including suppression of baseline Kv1.1 current density, and prominent current enhancement after holding at −120 mV (Figure 3F,G, increased currents between '1st' and 'last' pulses of a −120 mV train).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 3B,E-G.

claim: Slc7a5 is an important contributor to the Kv1.1 modulation observed in LM cells.
source: These findings indicate that Slc7a5 is an important contributor to the Kv1.1 modulation observed in LM cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the results section based on the knockdown and rescue experiments.

claim: Kv1.2 and Kv1.1 co-assemble to form heteromers.
source: Kv1.2 and Kv1.1 co-assemble to form heteromers (Al-Sabi et al., 2013; Coleman et al., 1999).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Kv1.2-Kv1.1 dimers exhibited a V1/2 of −25.5 ± 2.8 mV in parental LM cells and −24.2 ± 3.3 mV in ShR4-1.
source: Kv1.2-Kv1.1 dimers exhibited a V1/2 of −25.5 ± 2.8 mV in parental LM cells and −24.2 ± 3.3 mV in ShR4-1 (Figure 3—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 3—figure supplement 3A.

claim: Kv1.2-Kv1.1 linked channels did not undergo any current enhancement in either LM or ShR4-1 cell lines.
source: The linked channel did not undergo any current enhancement in either cell line (Figure 3—figure supplement 3B–D) indicating that sensitivity to endogenous Slc7a5 levels is not fully retained in Kv1.2-Kv1.1 heteromers.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 3—figure supplement 3B-D.

claim: Sensitivity to endogenous Slc7a5 levels is not fully retained in Kv1.2-Kv1.1 heteromers.
source: The linked channel did not undergo any current enhancement in either cell line (Figure 3—figure supplement 3B–D) indicating that sensitivity to endogenous Slc7a5 levels is not fully retained in Kv1.2-Kv1.1 heteromers.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the results section based on the experimental data.

claim: Overexpression of Slc7a5 in LM and ShR4-1 cells shifted Kv1.2-Kv1.1 channel activation by 30–35 mV.
source: Overexpression of Slc7a5 in LM and ShR4-1 cells shifted Kv1.2-Kv1.1 channel activation by 30–35 mV, along with pronounced inhibition that was relieved with a −120 mV holding voltage (Figure 3—figure supplement 3A–D).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 3—figure supplement 3A-D.

claim: Smaller effects observed in Kv1.2-Kv1.1 linked dimers relative to either homomeric channel suggests that subunit composition influences the functional outcome of Slc7a5 modulation.
source: We have not determined the stoichiometric requirement for the full Slc7a5-mediated gating shift in Kv1.2 (~−50 mV); however, smaller effects observed in Kv1.2-Kv1.1 linked dimers relative to either homomeric channel suggests that subunit composition influences the functional outcome of Slc7a5 modulation.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the results section based on the experimental data.

claim: Slc7a5-mediated amino acid transport is an important contributor to nutrient-dependent activation of mTORC1.
source: Slc7a5-mediated amino acid transport is an important contributor to nutrient-dependent activation of mTORC1 (Nicklin et al., 2009; Saxton and Sabatini, 2017; Wolfson et al., 2016, Wolfson et al., 2016), so a signal arising from Slc7a5-mediated transport could underlie Kv1 channel modulation (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Rapamycin treatment strongly inhibited basal mTORC1 signaling.
source: Untreated cells exhibited hallmarks of active mTORC1 (Figure 4B), in contrast to rapamycin treatment which strongly inhibited basal mTORC1 signaling. This was most obvious as suppression of phospho-S6 (p-S6), but also apparent in reduced levels of phospho-mTOR, and the appearance of lower molecular weight forms (likely due to dephosphorylation) of 4-EBP1 (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 4B.

claim: After rapamycin treatment, electrophysiological features of Slc7a5 modulation of Kv1.1 remained prominent.
source: However, after rapamycin treatment, electrophysiological features of Slc7a5 modulation of Kv1.1 remained prominent (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 4C.

claim: Rapamycin treatment did not alter baseline Kv1.1 current levels.
source: There was no alteration of baseline Kv1.1 current levels, and prominent relief of inhibition of Kv1.1 was observed (Figure 4C, increased currents between the 1st and last pulses of a −120 mV train).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 4C.

claim: Pharmacological suppression (by BCH) or shRNA knockdown of Slc7a5 did not influence p-S6 abundance or other markers of mTORC1 signaling in LM or ShR4-1 cells.
source: In LM or ShR4-1 cells, pharmacological suppression (by BCH) or shRNA knockdown of Slc7a5 did not influence p-S6 abundance or other markers of mTORC1 signaling (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Slc7a5-mediated gating effects were resistant to pharmacological inhibition by BCH.
source: However, even though Slc7a5 knockdown clearly attenuates Kv1.1 modulation (Figure 3), Slc7a5-mediated gating effects were resistant to pharmacological inhibition by BCH (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 4C.

claim: BCH or rapamycin did not influence the voltage-dependence of activation of Kv1.1.
source: Lastly, BCH or rapamycin did not influence the voltage-dependence of activation of Kv1.1 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B–D).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B-D.

claim: Amino acid transport or mTORC1 activation downstream of Slc7a5 are not required for modulation of Kv1 channels.
source: Taken together, Figure 4 illustrates that Slc7a5 is likely in close proximity to Kv1.1, and that amino acid transport or mTORC1 activation downstream of Slc7a5 are not required for modulation of Kv1 channels.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the results section based on the experimental data in Figure 4.

claim: Slc7a5 is likely in close proximity to Kv1.1.
source: Taken together, Figure 4 illustrates that Slc7a5 is likely in close proximity to Kv1.1, and that amino acid transport or mTORC1 activation downstream of Slc7a5 are not required for modulation of Kv1 channels.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the results section based on BRET data in Figure 4D-F.

claim: A BRET signal is detected between heterologously expressed Kv1.1 and Slc7a5.
source: We also detect a BRET signal between heterologously expressed Kv1.1 and Slc7a5 (Figure 4D–F).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 4D-F.

claim: The closely related transporter Slc7a6 did not generate a discernible BRET signal when co-expressed with Kv1.1-nanoluc.
source: In contrast, the closely related transporter Slc7a6 did not generate a discernible BRET signal (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 4F.

claim: Slc7a5 has no consistent effect on the extent of inactivation observed during 5 s depolarizing pulses (+40 mV) in Kv1.1 expressed in ShR4-1 cells.
source: In ShR4-1 cells transfected with Kv1.1, currents exhibit very slow inactivation, and Slc7a5 has no consistent effect on the extent of inactivation observed during 5 s depolarizing pulses (+40 mV, Figure 5A,B).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 5A,B.

claim: A transport-deficient Slc7a5[F252A] mutant has no consistent effect on Kv1.1 inactivation.
source: Building on previous experiments demonstrating that Kv1.1 modulation persists in the presence of the Slc7a5 inhibitor BCH (Figure 4), we also tested a transport-deficient Slc7a5[F252A] mutant (Singh and Ecker, 2018), which also has no consistent effect on Kv1.1 inactivation (Figure 5A,B).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 5A,B.

claim: Slc7a5 and Slc7a5[F252A] enhance the rate of inactivation of Kv1.1[Y379T].
source: We tested inactivation of the analogous mutation Kv1.1[Y379T] with Slc7a5 and Slc7a5[F252A] (Figure 5—figure supplement 1), and observed that Slc7a5 and Slc7a5[F252A] enhance the rate of inactivation, although this effect exhibited significant cell-to-cell variability (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The absence of effects of Slc7a5 on inactivation of WT Kv1.1 suggests that accelerated C-type inactivation does not underlie Slc7a5-mediated inhibition.
source: The absence of effects of Slc7a5 on inactivation of WT Kv1.1 suggests that accelerated C-type inactivation does not underlie Slc7a5-mediated inhibition.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the results section based on the experimental data in Figure 5.

claim: The effects of the Kv1.1[Y379T] mutation suggest that there may be some interplay between C-type inactivation and Slc7a5-mediated inhibition.
source: However, the effects of the Kv1.1[Y379T] mutation suggest that there may be some interplay between C-type inactivation and Slc7a5-mediated inhibition.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the results section based on the experimental data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Effects of Slc7a5 on the inactivation rate remain intact even after relieving Slc7a5-mediated inhibition of currents.
source: It is also noteworthy that effects of Slc7a5 on the inactivation rate (and the V1/2 of activation of Kv1.2 as reported in Baronas et al., 2018) remain intact even after relieving Slc7a5-mediated inhibition of currents.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and represents an observation from the experimental data.

claim: Strong hyperpolarizing stimuli allow channels to recover from an inhibited state, but do not 'break apart' the complex that underlies Slc7a5 modulation.
source: We interpret this to indicate that strong hyperpolarizing stimuli allow channels to recover from an inhibited state, but do not 'break apart' the complex that underlies Slc7a5 modulation.
evidence: This is an interpretation stated in the results section based on the experimental observations.

claim: Strong hyperpolarization to −120 mV was required to rescue currents from Slc7a5 inhibition after break-in.
source: Strong hyperpolarization to −120 mV was required to rescue currents from Slc7a5 inhibition after break-in (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Once Slc7a5-mediated inhibition was relieved, channels could recover from nearly complete inactivation with a holding potential of −80 mV.
source: However, once this inhibition was relieved, channels could recover from nearly complete inactivation with a holding potential of −80 mV (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A,C).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A,C.

claim: The disparity in the voltage-dependence of recovery from inactivation versus Slc7a5-mediated inhibition indicates that Slc7a5-mediated inhibition stabilizes channels by a mechanism distinct from C-type inactivation.
source: The disparity in the voltage-dependence of recovery from inactivation versus Slc7a5-mediated inhibition is summarized in Figure 6D, highlighting that nearly complete recovery from C-type inactivation (solid symbols, ratio of points e/d) is observed with a holding voltage of −80 mV, whereas this voltage does not recover Slc7a5-mediated inhibition (open symbols, ratio of points b/c). These findings indicate that Slc7a5-mediated inhibition stabilizes channels by a mechanism distinct from C-type inactivation.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the results section based on the experimental data in Figure 6.

claim: There appears to be some interaction between C-type inactivation and Slc7a5-mediated inhibition because Slc7a5 can influence the inactivation rate in channel mutants that are prone to C-type inactivation.
source: Nevertheless, there appears to be some interaction between these processes because Slc7a5 can influence the inactivation rate in channel mutants that are prone to C-type inactivation (Figure 5—figure supplement 1; Baronas et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the results section based on the experimental data.

claim: Kv1.5 exhibits no hallmarks of Slc7a5 modulation (i.e. no voltage shift or disinhibition).
source: Additionally, we have reported that Kv1.5 exhibits no hallmarks of Slc7a5 modulation (i.e. no voltage shift or disinhibition; Baronas et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The N-terminus, S1, and S2 segments of Kv1.2 can be replaced with Kv1.1 sequence, while still preserving a large Slc7a5-mediated shift in voltage-dependent gating.
source: The N-terminus, S1, and S2 segments of Kv1.2 can be replaced with Kv1.1 sequence, while still preserving a large Slc7a5-mediated shift in voltage-dependent gating (Figure 7A–D).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 7A-D.

claim: Further replacement of the S3 and S4 segments (and a small portion of the pore) in the Kv1.1S5/Kv1.2 chimera led to a significant switch toward a Kv1.1-like phenotype.
source: Further replacement of the S3 and S4 segments (and a small portion of the pore) in the Kv1.1S5/Kv1.2 chimera led to a significant switch toward a Kv1.1-like phenotype (Figure 7A,E), with a minimal Slc7a5-mediated gating shift and prominent current enhancement, even in the absence of transfected Slc7a5.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 7A,E.

claim: Introduction of the voltage-sensing domain of Kv1.2 into Kv1.1 (Kv1.2VSD/Kv1.1) transferred characteristic features of Kv1.2 modulation by Slc7a5.
source: Introduction of the voltage-sensing domain of Kv1.2 into Kv1.1 (Kv1.2VSD/Kv1.1) transferred characteristic features of Kv1.2 modulation by Slc7a5. These chimeric channels exhibited a prominent Slc7a5-dependent shift in voltage-dependent gating, and current disinhibition, comparable to Kv1.2 (Figure 7—figure supplement 2A,B).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 7—figure supplement 2A,B.

claim: Features of Slc7a5 modulation were absent when the Kv1.2VSD/Kv1.1 chimera was expressed alone.
source: In addition, these features of Slc7a5 modulation were absent when the Kv1.2VSD/Kv1.1 chimera was expressed alone (Figure 7—figure supplement 2A,B).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 7—figure supplement 2A,B.

claim: The Kv1.1VSD/Kv1.2 chimera exhibited prominent disinhibition of current even in the absence of Slc7a5.
source: The Kv1.1VSD/Kv1.2 chimera exhibited prominent disinhibition of current even in the absence of Slc7a5, and an attenuated shift in voltage dependence of activation when co-expressed with Slc7a5 (Figure 7—figure supplement 2C,D).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 7—figure supplement 2C,D.

claim: The Kv1.1VSD/Kv1.2 chimera exhibited an attenuated shift in voltage dependence of activation when co-expressed with Slc7a5.
source: The Kv1.1VSD/Kv1.2 chimera exhibited prominent disinhibition of current even in the absence of Slc7a5, and an attenuated shift in voltage dependence of activation when co-expressed with Slc7a5 (Figure 7—figure supplement 2C,D).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 7—figure supplement 2C,D.

claim: Channels became clearly resistant to Slc7a5-mediated gating shifts after the S1-S2 transmembrane helices of Kv1.2 were replaced with the sequence from Kv1.5.
source: Although Slc7a5-mediated gating shifts were sometimes variable, we observed that channels became clearly resistant to Slc7a5-mediated gating shifts after the S1-S2 transmembrane helices of Kv1.2 were replaced with the sequence from Kv1.5 (Figure 8—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 8—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Swapping the S1-S2 linker, S2 segment, or S2-S3 linker, had no consistent effect on the Slc7a5-mediated shift of Kv1.2 gating.
source: We generated conductance-voltage relationships for each of these chimeric channels (Figure 8—figure supplement 2A–D). Swapping the S1-S2 linker, S2 segment, or S2-S3 linker, had no consistent effect on the Slc7a5-mediated shift of Kv1.2 gating.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 8—figure supplement 2A-D.

claim: Replacing the S1 transmembrane segment of Kv1.2 with Kv1.5 sequence strongly attenuated the Slc7a5-mediated gating shift.
source: In contrast, replacing the S1 transmembrane segment of Kv1.2 with Kv1.5 sequence strongly attenuated the Slc7a5-mediated gating shift (Figure 8—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 8—figure supplement 2E.

claim: The Kv1.2[I164A] mutation near the intracellular boundary of S1 prominently attenuated the Slc7a5-mediated gating shift.
source: Conductance-voltage relationships for each mutant (Figure 8C–G) and a summary of V1/2 of activation (Figure 8B) reveal that most point mutants did not weaken Slc7a5-mediated effects. However, the Kv1.2[I164A] mutation near the intracellular boundary of S1 prominently attenuated the Slc7a5-mediated gating shift. (Figure 8B–G).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 8B-G.

claim: Position I164 in Kv1.2 strongly influences Slc7a5 sensitivity of Kv1 channels.
source: This highlights a single amino acid position that strongly influences Slc7a5 sensitivity of Kv1 channels.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the results section based on the experimental data in Figure 8.

claim: Kv1.1[V168I] retains Slc7a5 sensitivity.
source: Recordings in parental LM cells (with Slc7a5 modulation intact) illustrate that Kv1.1[V168I] (gray symbols) retains Slc7a5 sensitivity, as these channels exhibited suppressed currents upon break-in ('1st pulse'), along with prominent enhancement after holding at −120 mV ('last' pulse).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 9B.

claim: Kv1.1[V168A] exhibited large basal currents and comparably little current enhancement, suggesting weaker sensitivity to Slc7a5.
source: In contrast, Kv1.1[V168A] (green) exhibited large basal currents and comparably little current enhancement, suggesting weaker sensitivity to Slc7a5 (Figure 9B, summarized in lower panel).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 9B.

claim: Outcomes of V168 mutants are strongly influenced by the presence of Slc7a5, rather than effects on intrinsic channel function.
source: In ShR4-1 cells (Figure 9D), effects of V168 mutations are blunted, illustrating that outcomes of V168 mutants are strongly influenced by the presence of Slc7a5, rather than effects on intrinsic channel function.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the results section based on the experimental data in Figure 9D.

claim: Slc7a5 is expressed in a wide variety of cell types and undergoes prominent changes in certain physiological or pathological conditions.
source: Slc7a5 is expressed in a wide variety of cell types and undergoes prominent changes in certain physiological or pathological conditions.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section and represents general knowledge about Slc7a5.

claim: T cell activation and proliferation requires prominent upregulation of Slc7a5.
source: For example, T cell activation and proliferation requires prominent upregulation of Slc7a5, leading to protein abundance orders of magnitude larger than Kv channel expression (Marchingo et al., 2020; Sinclair et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section and supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Slc7a5 upregulation has been reported in a variety of tumor types.
source: Slc7a5 upregulation has also been reported in a variety of tumor types (Barollo et al., 2016), and Slc7a5 inhibition attenuates proliferation of cells (Salisbury and Arthur, 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section and supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Slc7a5 inhibition attenuates proliferation of cells.
source: Slc7a5 upregulation has also been reported in a variety of tumor types (Barollo et al., 2016), and Slc7a5 inhibition attenuates proliferation of cells (Salisbury and Arthur, 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section and supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Changes in ion channel activity and cellular excitability are linked to cell division and proliferation in normal development and cancer or other pathologies.
source: However, changes in ion channel activity and cellular excitability are also linked to cell division and proliferation in normal development and cancer or other pathologies (Huang and Jan, 2014; Pardo and Stühmer, 2014; Satou et al., 2020; Serrano-Novillo et al., 2019; Yang et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section and supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The inhibitory effect of Slc7a5 on Kv1.1 and Kv1.2 may enhance excitability in neuropathic pain.
source: Recent work has also suggested that the inhibitory effect of Slc7a5 on Kv1.1 and Kv1.2 may enhance excitability in neuropathic pain (Alles et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section and supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Gene expression of Slc7a5 overlaps with Kv1.1/1.2 in the NF1-3 subclass of DRG neurons and INH2 subclass of spinal cord neurons.
source: Gene expression (mousebrain.org) of Slc7a5 overlaps with Kv1.1/1.2 in the NF1-3 subclass of DRG neurons and INH2 subclass of spinal cord neurons, each with varying degrees of expression between cell types.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section and represents data from a gene expression database.

claim: Excitability in certain cell types in the nervous system may be influenced by Slc7a5-mediated regulation of Kv1 channels.
source: Therefore, excitability in certain cell types in the nervous system may be influenced by Slc7a5-mediated regulation of Kv1 channels, and altered during pain and inflammation.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the discussion section based on the experimental findings and prior work.

claim: Differential sensitivity, expression, and assembly of Kv1 isoforms and Slc7a5 may fine tune the interplay between channel and transporter.
source: Overall, differential sensitivity, expression, and assembly of Kv1 isoforms and Slc7a5 may fine tune the interplay between channel and transporter.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the discussion section based on the experimental findings.

claim: The canonical auxiliary subunits of the Kv1 channel family are the Kvβ subunits.
source: The canonical auxiliary subunits of the Kv1 channel family are the Kvβ subunits, which are soluble proteins that interact with a cytoplasmic scaffolding domain that is structurally distinct from the Kv1 transmembrane domains (Gulbis et al., 2000; Long et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section and supported by citations to prior work.

claim: BK channels can be modulated simultaneously by both the BKβ and BKγ subunits.
source: BK channels can be modulated simultaneously by both the BKβ and BKγ subunits, which are thought to associate with the pore-forming subunits via transmembrane domains (Gonzalez-Perez et al., 2015; Gonzalez-Perez and Lingle, 2019; Yan and Aldrich, 2012, Yan and Aldrich, 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section and supported by citations to prior work.

claim: KCNE subunits have been proposed to integrate into clefts between neighboring voltage-sensing domains to modulate channel function.
source: Similarly, the widely studied KCNE subunits are transmembrane proteins that have been proposed to integrate into clefts between neighboring voltage-sensing domains to modulate channel function (Murray et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2012; Xu et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section and supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Kv4 channels are sensitive to both KChIP (a soluble cytoplasmic protein) and DPP-like proteins (transmembrane), leading to modulation of channel expression and gating.
source: Another Kv channel with prominent regulation of channel gating by multiple classes of regulatory proteins is the Kv4 family, which is sensitive to both KChIP (a soluble cytoplasmic protein) and DPP-like proteins (transmembrane), leading to modulation of channel expression and gating (Jerng et al., 2005; Kitazawa et al., 2015; Zagha et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section and supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Kv1.2 is co-regulated by Slc7a5 and Kvβ subunits.
source: Our previous studies have demonstrated co-regulation of Kv1.2 by Slc7a5 and Kvβ subunits (Baronas et al., 2018; Lamothe and Kurata, 2020), indicating the possibility that Kv1 channels might assemble with multiple accessory subunits simultaneously (similar to the putative Kv4 complex with KChIP and DPP-like proteins).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section and supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Kv1.2 gating is powerfully regulated by extracellular redox conditions, by a mechanism that is not intrinsic to the Kv1.2 α-subunit.
source: It is also noteworthy that we have previously identified powerful regulation of Kv1.2 gating by extracellular redox conditions, by a mechanism that is not intrinsic to the Kv1.2 α-subunit (Baronas et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section and supported by citation to prior work.

claim: A recent study has suggested a possible role for the sigma opioid receptor in Kv1.2 regulation.
source: This effect is vastly different from Slc7a5 modulation, indicating an additional regulatory mechanism, and a recent study has suggested a possible role for the sigma opioid receptor (Abraham et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section and supported by citation to prior work.
